title: Performing for engaged audiences and call and response
summary: Audience energy and call and response in New Orleans music and second line dancing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yesterday you played in Utica. And I was wondering, because both you and your drummer were talking about how joyful and active this New Orleans music is. And is it different to perform for an audience that maybe isn’t as engaged as an audience in New Orleans might be?

Yeah. I think it’s always good for us if the audience is engaged. You know we feed off of that energy. In New Orleans that’s very common when you’re performing or if it’s a parade, or whatever it is, when — it’s like Gerald was speaking about call and response in the music yesterday. When something is done, somebody else takes up where that’s left off. And it’s always a conversation. If it’s the music, or if you ever watched a second line dancers dancing, you know if you see one person doing one dance, then someone else takes over and starts right where that person left off, for lack of a better way to explain it. Yeah. So it’s important for us when the audience is engaged and we’re getting that feedback from them. If we see them moving around, you know, we know that we’re moving their spirit and that’s what we intend to do. The reciprocal of that is then it moves us as well.
